newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish Islamist PM Erbakan faces rising pressure.
newsitem.headline: Turkish Islamist PM Erbakan faces rising pressure.

text.p: Turkey's secularist majority joined ranks on Monday with the pro-Western army in an assault on Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist ambitions.
Several thousand anti-Islamist demonstrators took to the streets of Istanbul and a veteran politician warned Erbakan to respect democracy and toe the official secularist line.
"I told him that if he can't do that then he should leave the government," leftist leader and former prime minister Bulent Ecevit told a news conference after meeting Erbakan.
A recent increase in army criticism of the coalition has stirred memories of three military coups in the last 37 years.
But Erbakan brushed off the generals' latest efforts to influence the running of the country.
"In Turkey governments are formed in parliament, not in the National Security Council. Laws are made in parliament," he told reporters at the parliament offices of his Welfare Party.
The military-dominated council warned Erbakan at the weekend to end a recent surge in religious activism they fear could pave the way to turning NATO member Turkey into an Islamist state.

At a later news conference Erbakan blamed the media for creating "artificial tension" and said Welfare was working in harmony with the constitution. "The Welfare Party does not have the slightest problem with the regime," Erbakan said.
Erbakan held an unscheduled meeting with Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller at 6.45 p.m. (1645 GMT), the state-run Anatolian news agency reported.
Turkish stocks dived 5.58 percent at the close of trading on the political uncertainty.
"An easing in political tension is needed. Newspapers full of pictures of army generals negatively affect the market," said broker Mustafa Yilmaz.
A prominent member of Welfare called for the government to heed the army warning.
"Welfare should take steps to smooth this out," the Yeni Yuzyil paper quoted MP Aydin Menderes as saying. Menderes' father Adnan was executed after a 1960 coup that deposed him as prime minister.
Erbakan, 70, became modern Turkey's first Islamist leader last year in alliance with conservatives after narrowly winning general elections with 21 percent of the vote.
Many secularists say he has no mandate to raise the profile of Islam in public life, one of Turkey's most sensitive issues.

Several thousand people, mostly women, sang republican marching songs and chanted anti-government slogans in Istanbul's central Taksim Square at a ceremony to mark the anniversary of a key date in Turkey's secularist calendar.

Military leader Kemal Ataturk scrapped the 1,300-year-old caliphate of Sunni Islam on March 3, 1924 as part of wideranging Westernising reforms. The caliphate had last been held by the Turkish Ottoman sultans overthrown by Ataturk.
Today's generals want the government to enforce 1920s republican laws such as bans on Islamic headwear and Moslem sects. The legislation has been largely ignored in recent years.

Demonstrators laid flowers at a statue of Ataturk, witnesses said. "Turkey is secular and will stay secular," protesters sang in Taksim Square, where Welfare plans to build a large mosque in an apparent challenge to the secularists.
The army briefly sent tanks onto the streets of an Islamist district of Ankara last month after anti-secularist protest there attended by the Iranian ambassador.
Erbakan faces an opposition censure vote in parliament on Tuesday. His coalition with free-marketeer Ciller has a majority of around half a dozen in the 550-seat assembly.
